log.note: Raised from the urbarial tables in folder F-011.

A Roman Catholic woman born at Szenna in 1816 is the wife of the oldest Solymos Duska in 1869. The two villages married into each other. It does not show a Duska moving to Senné. The census sheets for Senné houses 5 and 6 would: they should give the birthplaces of both György Duskas (request R-014).
By the 1890s county map Solymos and Szenna are about 4 km apart, not the 6 km written when this was raised, with marsh between them and a district line. Nearer, but distance alone moves nothing.
With György Duska the elder entered as Ahn 32, this is now the question of where Ahn 32 was born.

Duskas were at Szenna by 1829 and they were Greek Catholic, like the György Duska born at Solymos in 1820 and unlike the Reformed majority of the name there. The tables of about 1770 show none at Szenna. That fits a move from Solymos between about 1770 and 1829; it does not show one.
Duskas born about 1798 to 1803 lived and died at Senné. If the family came from Solymos it came before 1800, which the urbarial tables of about 1770 neither show nor rule out.

A test now exists that paper could not offer: the owner's Y branch is known (S-000-18). A male-line descendant of the Reformed Duskas of Solymos who tested would show whether the two families share a father within the last few centuries. Nobody has; the hypothesis stays at 30.

The owner's hired translator looked at the Reformed György Dusko of Solymos, born 1852, as a possible father of András and wrote 'I didn't found a connection' (D-015-12). That is one man's negative on one candidate, and the candidate was the wrong generation: András's father was born about 1833. It says nothing either way on whether the two families share an older root.

The grandfather's 3,000 strongest matches hold no other Duska in any spelling (D-016-18). So no descendant of the Reformed Duskas of Solymos, or of any Duska, has a kit on that site close enough to show. It is an absence in one database, not evidence against kinship.

log.note: At the cap for a link without an archive reference (X-009). It shows a Roman Catholic Duska of Senné, house 6, in a French-language cemetery, which is what would be expected of a kinsman of Mike Duska of Montréal. It does not say which Mihály Mike was.
Mike Duska lived at 1196a St. George Street, Montréal, in 1937. If the cemetery of record FT 01965 is in Montréal, Miklós and Mike were in one city.

Mikulas Duska of Senné, 39, is on the passenger list with Michal, and was naturalised in Canada on 21 January 1946: so Miklós did go to Canada. But his wife in the census is Maria, born 1892, and the cemetery record names a spouse Anna Hancosek. A second marriage, or a wrong field, or a different man. Kept at 70.

The census of 1940 gives the maiden name of Mikuláš Duška's wife at Senné 11 as Hankoščáková, the 'Hancosek' of the cemetery record, and lists Mikuláš among the absent. The surname now agrees and the given name (Mária here, Anna there) does not. With the birth date and the Canadian naturalisation of 1946 the identification is firm in substance; it stays at the cap because the cemetery is still unnamed.

Štefan's godmother in 1929 was Zuzanna Bandura née Hankoščák of Senné (D-006-21): the Hankoščák family stood close to both Duska households. Mike Duska was buried in Côte-des-Neiges cemetery; whether plot FT 01965 is there is still not shown.
The cemetery paper is a database printout, not a burial register. Its stand-in dates are a property of the object.

The index adds nothing on who he was, but it removes one of the three points against: the cemetery is named, and it is the one where his travelling companion Michal Duska was buried nine years later. The wife's name is again Hancosek (D-013-100).

A Miklós Duska was at Senné in March 1921 with a wife named Hankovcsák (D-013-172); her family's surname is the one the Montréal cemetery wrote Hancosek, and her likely father, the bell-ringer, has a burial with it spelled out (D-013-195). The Senné man and the Montréal man share a name, a birth date and a wife's surname.

One of its legs is weaker. The case began with a birth date on the cemetery's printout that matches the Senné baptism to the day. The cemetery now writes that before the 1980s it recorded almost no dates of birth (D-014-08). The printed date is exactly 75 years before the day of arrival, so it may have been computed from an age of 75 and not copied from a paper. If so, it shows a man of about 75, not a man born on that day. Miklós would have turned 75 on 28 November 1965, which still fits. What carries the link now: the rare surname, the given name, the wife's surname (Hancosek for Hankovcsák), and Mikulas and Michal Duska on one passenger list.

A second set of books has the birth date. The Québec death index gives Mikalis Duska born 28-11-1890 and died 28-11-1965 (D-015-09). At B-053 I lowered this because the cemetery said it kept almost no birth dates then, so its printed date might have been made up from the day he arrived. The civil index is not the cemetery's book, and it calls 28 November 1965 the date of death. The date of birth stands on two records in Montréal and on the baptism at Szenna 6 (D-015-07). What is still missing is a paper that says the Montréal man came from Senné.

The owner asked himself in 2022 whether one or two men called Miklós came to Montréal (D-014-10). The strips hold one Miklós Duska born at Senné about 1890. His list also has a 'Miklo Duska, maybe, born about 1890, who travelled to the US in 1913'; if that is the same man he crossed twice, and the passenger strip of 1930 would be a second voyage. Nothing in hand for 1913.

statement: The Duska male line was East Slavic (Rusyn) and Greek Catholic when it reached Szenna, and came into Ung county from the north or east; it is not a Magyar line and not one from western Slovakia.
basis: Paper: the oldest Duskas at Szenna are in the Greek Catholic book, a Joannes who died in 1830 aged 61 and a Georgius dead before 1874 (H-079, at 70); the Roman Catholic Duskas appear in the books a generation later. The Duskas of Solymos, the next village, were Reformed by the 1790s (H-063, H-064), which cuts the other way: a Reformed family in Ung is more often Magyar or long settled. Rite is not origin: a line can change church at one marriage. The paper alone stood at about 50. DNA (S-000-18, L-027): the owner's Y branch lies in a part of R1a that the Demko agent's note describes as commonest among East Slavs and Balts and scarce among Slovaks and Hungarians. That leans the same way and adds about five. It cannot add more: the branch formed about 400 BCE, the one placed sample on it is from north-central Poland, no man on it bears the surname, and nobody within the reach of the registers has tested. Against: a branch this old says nothing of the last three hundred years, and it cannot tell a Rusyn from a Slovak of the same valley.
test: A Y test by a second male-line Duska, best a descendant of the Reformed Duskas of Solymos or of another Senné branch: a match in the last few hundred years would also settle H-057 and H-042, which no record in hand can. On paper: the Places agent's settlement history of Senné; the tax lists of 1715 and 1720 for a Duska in Ung; the Greek Catholic book that served Szenna before 1829.

log.note: Raised on ledger v26 (X-023, rewritten), which opens the owner's own Y result to this line and lets it move a hypothesis of origin and nothing else. No person is named by it and no identity or parent link moves on it.

Admixture figures for the owner's grandfather Steve (D-016-02, -04, -06, -10, -14). Five calculators agree on a man of east-central European stock with a small eastern part: Siberian 2.35 (K13), 2.14 (K9), 1.93 (MDLP); Volga-Ural 3.2 (K36); East Eurasian 5.99 against the owner's own 3.8 to 4.1 (Gedrosia). That is in keeping with a Carpathian or East Slavic origin and with what the registers say of all four of his grandparents. It is about the whole man, his Demko half as much as his Duska half, and says nothing of the male line as such. It cannot tell a Rusyn from a Slovak. Not moved.

The grandfather's file confirms that the owner's Y chromosome is Štefan's: 1,638 markers of 1,638 (D-016-17). So the Y result of S-000-18 belongs to the Duska male line at least as far up as Ahn 4, on evidence and not only on the tree. The origin of that line is where it was.

The surnames near the top of the grandfather's match list are largely Carpathian: Slovak, Rusyn, Polish, Hungarian (D-016-18). That is where his cousins' families came from, on both his sides. An impression from names, not a count, and it does not separate the Duska side from the Demko side.
